title: The fourth jhana
hookLine: a person wrapped head to foot in clean white cloth (MN 39)

cards: A clean white cloth, fresh off the line, still cool. Someone sits down, and the cloth is drawn over them from the top of the head to the soles of the feet. Not to hide them.
Just to cover them evenly, all the way around. No part warmer than another. No part left out.
Almost nothing happens in this picture, and that's the point. It's the last of the Buddha's four pictures of deep concentration.

teach.h: PLEASURE AND PAIN BOTH LET GO.
teach.b: MN 39 describes it this way. Pleasure and pain are both let go, as gladness and sorrow faded earlier.
What's left is neither painful nor pleasant: mindfulness made pure by equanimity.

teach.h: WRAPPED HEAD TO FOOT IN WHITE.
teach.b: A person sits pervading the body with a pure, bright mind, like someone wrapped from the head down in white cloth, so that no part of the body is uncovered. Look at the path the four jhanas trace. First, thinking settles.
Then the bubbling joy fades. Now even pleasure is let go. Each stage is less, not more, and what's left is plain as the cloth: no pattern, no color, nothing to grab.
Strangely, the suttas treat this not as an ending but as a platform.
In MN 36, the Buddha says that on the night of his awakening, his mind concentrated like this, pure and bright, steady and pliable, he directed it toward knowledge, and the three knowledges followed.
And in DN 16, the Great Discourse on the Final Nibbana, his last moments pass through the jhanas, and he passes away on emerging from the fourth.
So the week ends here: the quail on its own ground, the monkey and the pitch, then right concentration in four pictures.
Bath powder soaked through, a lake fed by a spring, lotuses under water, a person wrapped in white. Each quieter than the last.

how: In Theravada teaching the fourth jhana is often described as the basis for insight and the higher knowledges; meditators who work with the jhanas usually do so under a teacher; the suttas tell both the Buddha's awakening and his final passing with the fourth jhana.

o: a trance where awareness switches off completely
the most blissful state a meditator can reach
deep stillness past pleasure and pain, in equanimity

games.q: match each jhana to its picture.
p: a lake fed by a spring
wrapped head to foot in white

s: the fourth jhana is the most pleasant of the four
even pleasure is let go; it's neither painful nor pleasant, with pure mindfulness.
in MN 36, the Buddha turns his concentrated mind toward knowledge on the night of awakening
the pure, bright mind became a platform for the three knowledges.
DN 16 tells that the Buddha passed away on emerging from the fourth jhana
his last moments pass through the jhanas.

games.q: your mind is still, pure and bright, covered by equanimity like a white cloth. in MN 36, what does the Buddha-to-be do next?
o: stays there as long as possible
directs the clear mind toward knowledge
gets up and goes to find food
games.why: he directed it toward knowledge, and the three knowledges of the night of awakening followed. the stillness was a platform, not the destination.

practice: Let your attention cover the body evenly, head to foot, the way the cloth covers, with no spot more interesting than another.
If something itches, it can itch; if something is pleasant, it can be pleasant, with no chasing and no pushing away. Rest in the middle, and let it all be covered by plain, clear knowing.

wordCard.voice: Fourth jhana. The last of the four deep meditative absorptions: neither pleasure nor pain, only equanimity and mindfulness, like a body wrapped evenly in white cloth.

orig.note: Pali upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi: purity of mindfulness through equanimity, the mark of the fourth jhāna.

carryVoice: Your line: wrapped in white. In the suttas, this stillness is where seeing begins. Go gently.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 39, Maha-Assapura Sutta (the white cloth simile)
Majjhima Nikaya 36, Mahasaccaka Sutta (the night of awakening)
Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta (the Buddha's final passing)
